notes: Setup wizard: the first person to open the site and register becomes the owner, so register right after the install. Firefly III runs in single-user mode by default, so registration closes once that first account exists; the owner can invite more users from the administration pages.
APP_KEY must be exactly 32 characters (Firefly III's own rule), so it is a plain generated secret rather than base64. The image runs the database migrations and upgrades itself on every start.

Three services: the Firefly III app (the only published port), MariaDB 11.8 (the official file uses mariadb:lts) and a tiny cron service. The official file runs crond in an Alpine container that installs tzdata from the internet on every start; here a plain Alpine loop calls /api/v1/cron/<STATIC_CRON_TOKEN> on the app one hour after it starts and then every 24 hours (recurring transactions, auto-budgets, bill reminders and webhooks), which is the daily schedule upstream asks for. Firefly III also skips a job that ran less than 12 hours earlier. The token travels in the HTTP request on stdin of nc, never in a command line that ps could show. The request side stays open for up to 300 seconds (sleep 300 inside the pipe) because BusyBox nc closes the connection as soon as its input ends, and the app then drops the request unanswered (measured: HTTP 499, no job ran); the loop sleeps 3600 + 300 + 82500 seconds, one day in total.
STATIC_CRON_TOKEN is a generated 32-character secret, the exact length Firefly III requires. It only lets someone trigger those daily jobs early.

Behind the panel's HTTPS proxy, TRUSTED_PROXIES='**' (the value Firefly III's .env.example recommends for Docker) makes it trust the forwarded https scheme and host. APP_URL is the site's HTTPS address.

Mail goes to the application log (MAIL_MAILER=log) until you set the MAIL_* variables for an SMTP server in the panel's environment editor, so password-reset and bill-reminder emails are not sent before that. LOG_CHANNEL=stdout sends the log to the container log.
The upload volume holds attachments; everything else is in MariaDB. Back up both.
